draft.title: Experimenting with punctuation
card: Authors sometimes leave out or bend punctuation on purpose. This is a choice, not a mistake, and it changes how the text reads.
Dropping speech marks can blend speech into the narration. It can make a voice feel like thought or memory.
A long run of words with few commas or full stops can feel rushed, breathless or overwhelmed.
A dash, a string of dots or a sudden stop can make a voice sound hesitant or cut off.
draft.remember: Unusual punctuation is a choice that shapes voice, rhythm or feeling.

a.q: A writer describes a panicked girl running late. The list of things she grabs has no commas between the items. What is the effect of leaving out the commas?
opts: It creates a rushed, breathless rhythm
It shows the writer forgot the commas
It slows the pace to a calm, steady beat
It makes the girl sound hesitant and unsure
a.why: With no commas the words run together, so the reader cannot pause, which suits panic. Slowing the pace is wrong because the missing pauses speed the reading up.
a.clue: Commas give the reader a pause. What happens without them?

b.q: In a novel, a narrator recalls her grandfather's words with no speech marks, so they sit inside the narration. What is the most likely effect?
opts: His words feel like part of her memory
His words become clearer and more formal
His words sound like a loud argument
His words become harder to believe as true
b.why: Without speech marks the speech blends into the narration, so it feels like something remembered. It does not make the words more formal, because speech marks are what usually mark speech as separate.
b.clue: Think about speech blending into the narrator's own voice.

a.best: It creates a rushed, breathless rhythm

b.best: His words feel like part of her memory
